messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Sarah

Sarah was thirty-two when she witnessed her younger brother Marcus being shot by a police officer during a traffic stop in a parking garage in downtown Los Angeles. She had been waiting in his car while he ran into a store; when he returned, a patrol car pulled alongside them. What followed unfolded in fragments that her mind still could not assemble into a coherent sequence. There was shouting. Marcus reaching toward the glove compartment—she could not remember why, could not articulate what he had said or done in the seconds before. The officer's hand on his weapon. Then the sound, which she heard before she understood what it meant. Marcus collapsed against the passenger door. The officer's face. His partner's radio crackling. The blood on the window that Sarah could not stop seeing when she closed her eyes, even three years later.

The officer was never charged. An internal review concluded the shooting was justified. Sarah attended every hearing, sat in courtrooms where officials she did not recognize explained why her brother's death was permissible, and she left each time feeling as though the world had rewritten itself into a place where such things simply happened, where there was no recourse, no accountability. She had come to believe that the people responsible had faced no consequences, and this knowledge had calcified into something deeper—a conviction that she lived in a fundamentally unsafe world where violence could erupt without warning and where those who caused it walked free. What frightened her most was not the memory of that day itself, but the certainty that it could happen again, that no one could protect her, that even when her therapist or her few remaining friends told her she was safe, they were wrong or naive or simply did not understand.

Three years on, Sarah was thirty-five and working sporadically as an actor in television and commercial work, though the industry had become increasingly difficult to navigate. She was certain now that she was permanently an outsider—not just in the world at large, but among the people around her who had not witnessed what she had witnessed. No one else carried this knowledge. No one else understood that safety was an illusion. She felt isolated and set apart, and this feeling had begun to reshape how she moved through her life. In audition waiting rooms, she positioned herself in corners where she could see the door and count the exits, always choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected she felt. On set, she found herself scanning for uniforms, for weapons, for anything that might trigger the fragmented pieces of memory that came without warning—the disconnected images and sounds that would not cohere into a story she could tell or process. When she tried to describe the shooting to a casting director who had asked why she seemed anxious during a police procedural audition, the words simply would not come. She could not put the frightening event into words, could only offer vague apologies and excuses.

The fragmented quality of her memories—the way they arrived as sensory shards rather than narrative—had begun to feed her conviction that the world was fundamentally chaotic and untrustworthy. Each time a piece of that day surfaced unbidden, it reinforced her sense that nothing could be predicted or controlled, that safety was a fantasy others clung to. When she remembered the frightening event, she felt like it was happening right now, and the intensity of that reliving had convinced her that her appraisals were correct—that danger was real and constant. She had started avoiding public transport, where she could not control her surroundings or choose her seat. She avoided anywhere she might see uniforms or weapons. These avoidances had made sense at first, a way of protecting herself from triggers that sent her spiraling into that garage, into the moment before the shot. But over months, the avoidance had tightened around her life like a net. She had turned down roles that required scenes in police stations or military settings. She had stopped taking the bus to auditions, instead spending money she did not have on rideshares and taxis. She had begun to spend impulsively—on clothes she did not wear, on books she did not read, on anything that offered a moment of distraction or comfort. The spending left her depleted, financially and emotionally, and each purchase reinforced her sense of herself as someone out of control, someone broken, someone who did not belong in the world as it was.

The avoidance and the spending had become their own kind of trap. By avoiding situations that triggered her memories, she had inadvertently confirmed her belief that those situations were genuinely dangerous, that her fear was justified. By spending to soothe herself, she had accumulated debt and shame, which deepened her conviction that she was fundamentally isolated—that no one else struggled this way, that her coping mechanisms were signs of her own weakness or damage. She had not worked in six weeks. Her agent had stopped calling. The negative emotions—the fear, the horror, the guilt that she had survived when Marcus had not, the shame of her own unraveling—had become so constant that she could barely distinguish them from her baseline. She came to therapy because a friend had finally, after months of gentle insistence, convinced her that something had to change. Sarah sat in the waiting room, choosing a chair that faced the door, her hands trembling slightly, uncertain whether talking about any of this could possibly help, but terrified of what would happen if she did not try.
